documents.unit: Dean of Students, Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities
documents.title: AI Academic Misconduct
documents.summary: Faculty-facing guidance from the Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities on academic misconduct, with AI as one concern. It lists unauthorized AI use as misconduct, asks instructors to state whether AI is allowed and how to cite it, and walks them through reporting and outcomes.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no university rule on whether AI is allowed. It lists "Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence or online resources" as misconduct and says faculty "should clearly state: Whether AI tools are permitted", so the decision is handed to instructors: delegates.

units.why: The opening sentence gives the reason for the page: integrity is grounded in "honesty, trust, fairness, respect and responsibility". It states a principle rather than a rule, so it is informs/general; P95 (fairness and honesty as the ground for AI rules) fits better than P41 because no skill-building is mentioned.
units.anchor: supports a learning environment grounded in honesty, trust, fairness, respect and responsibility
units.fit_note: The sentence is about academic integrity in general, not AI specifically; the page is about AI misconduct.

units.why: The page lists faculty duties: "Clearly communicate academic expectations". It binds instructors and happens at course start; P09 (state expectations in the syllabus) is the nearest type, but it names no syllabus and no AI.
units.anchor: Clearly communicate academic expectations
units.fit_note: General duty to communicate academic expectations; AI is not named here and the syllabus is not mentioned.

units.why: The list of duties says faculty are "expected to" "Submit reports when violations are suspected". It addresses instructors once misuse is suspected, so when-misuse; P81 (formal reporting procedure) fits.
units.anchor: Submit reports when violations are suspected
units.frag_start: Submit reports when violations are suspected
units.frag_end: Submit reports when violations are suspected

units.why: The page says misconduct "may include" "Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence or online resources". That classifies improper AI use as misconduct, which is P36; it is a definition of misuse so modality informs and unit_stance restrict (AI is barred unless authorized).
units.anchor: Unauthorized use of artificial intelligence or online resources

units.why: Faculty "are encouraged to" "Review academic integrity expectations at the beginning of the semester". This is about when to communicate expectations (course-start) and is a recommendation, so should; P09 is the nearest type though it is not strictly about a syllabus.
units.anchor: Review academic integrity expectations at the beginning of the semester
units.fit_note: Asks for expectations to be reviewed at semester start (and before major assignments), not necessarily written in the syllabus.

units.why: Faculty are encouraged to "Clarify expectations regarding AI tools, online resources, and citation practices". It tells instructors to make AI expectations explicit, which is P09; the decision itself is left to them.
units.anchor: Clarify expectations regarding AI tools, online resources, and citation practices

units.why: The text says faculty "are encouraged to include a syllabus statement" that "Explains course-specific expectations (i.e. acceptable A.I. Use)". It asks for a syllabus statement covering AI, so P09 with should; it is encouraged, not required.
units.anchor: Explains course-specific expectations (i.e. acceptable A.I. Use)
units.fit_note: Encouraged rather than required; the statement also references the Student Code, defines prohibited behaviors and outlines consequences.

units.why: Among "areas to clarify" the page lists "Use of generative AI tools" alongside exam format and group work. It treats generative AI as one item instructors decide per course, so P04 (instructor sets the rule) fits better than P09, which is about the statement itself.
units.anchor: Use of generative AI tools
units.frag_start: Examples of areas to clarify include

units.why: Faculty "should clearly state" "Whether AI tools are permitted" and "What types of assistance are allowed". The university sets no default and hands the permission decision to each instructor, so P04; actor is instructor.
units.anchor: Whether AI tools are permitted

units.why: The same list asks for "Citation expectations for AI-generated content". It tells instructors to say how AI should be cited, which is closest to P24 (disclose/cite AI); the page itself does not require students to cite.
units.anchor: Citation expectations for AI-generated content
units.fit_note: Instructors are told to state citation expectations; the page does not itself require students to disclose or cite AI.

units.why: The sentence "Students should not be expected to guess what is or is not permitted in a course" gives the reason for the preceding duty. It is a principle of fairness about clarity, so informs; P09 is the best home because it justifies stating rules explicitly.
units.anchor: Students should not be expected to guess what is or is not permitted
units.fit_note: States the rationale for explicit course rules rather than the duty itself.

units.why: The page says faculty "may wish to emphasize" the reasons integrity matters, and notes students "are more likely to make ethical decisions when they understand the broader impact". That is explaining the rules to students, which is P66.
units.anchor: Students are more likely to make ethical decisions when they understand

units.why: Faculty may emphasize that "Academic integrity protects the value of a UWF degree". The reason offered is protecting the credential and fairness to peers, not skill-building, so P95 rather than P41.
units.anchor: Academic integrity protects the value of a UWF degree

units.why: Faculty "can reduce opportunities for misconduct" by "Using varied or personalized assignment prompts" and similar steps. These are assignment redesign measures (P35) addressed to instructors before the course.
units.anchor: Using varied or personalized assignment prompts
units.frag_start: Faculty can reduce opportunities for misconduct
units.fit_note: General misconduct-prevention advice, not specific to AI.

units.why: The item "Structuring assessments that emphasize process over memorization" suggests grading and design built on process. P35 covers grading around process; modality may because it is an option in a list of "can" steps.
units.anchor: Structuring assessments that emphasize process over memorization

units.why: "Utilizing question banks and randomized testing" is listed as a way to reduce misconduct in exams. It changes assessment design, so P35 fits better than P33 since it does not move weight to proctored work.
units.anchor: Utilizing question banks and randomized testing
units.frag_start: Utilizing question banks and randomized testing
units.fit_note: Exam integrity measure, not specific to AI.

units.why: The page says "Academic pressure, time management difficulties, and stress can contribute to misconduct" and encourages reminding students of resources. This is prevention by easing causes of misuse, so P99; pointing to tutoring and offices (P72) is the next unit, so I chose P99 for the stated purpose.
units.anchor: Academic pressure, time management difficulties, and stress can contribute to misconduct.

units.why: Faculty are encouraged to remind students of "Tutoring and academic support services", "Writing assistance" and "Office hours". This directs students to human help, P72; P99 is used for the preceding rationale sentence.
units.anchor: Tutoring and academic support services

units.why: Faculty "are encouraged to communicate with the student before submitting a report". That is talking before escalating, P57; it covers suspected misuse (when-misuse) and is a recommendation.
units.anchor: faculty are encouraged to communicate with the student before submitting a report

units.why: The sentence "Faculty should remain professional, objective and focused on the observed behavior and available information" sets an evidence stance for suspected misconduct, closest to P69; it does not set a standard of proof, so fit is partial.
units.anchor: focused on the observed behavior and available information
units.fit_note: Asks for objectivity and reliance on observed behavior; sets no standard of proof or list of acceptable evidence.

units.why: The page lists what to include when reporting: "Description of the suspected misconduct", "Supporting documentation". This is the reporting procedure, P81, addressed to instructors.
units.anchor: When reporting suspected academic misconduct, include:

units.why: Examples of supporting documentation include "Turnitin or plagiarism reports" and "Canvas activity logs". These are similarity checks and activity logs used as evidence, P40; the page names no AI detector.
units.anchor: Turnitin or plagiarism reports
units.frag_end: Examples of supporting documentation may include:
units.fit_note: Lists Turnitin/plagiarism reports and Canvas activity logs as evidence of misconduct generally; AI detectors are not named.

units.why: The text says "Reports should be submitted as promptly as possible after discovery of the concern" via "the appropriate university reporting process". A deadline and process for reporting is P81.
units.anchor: Reports should be submitted as promptly as possible after discovery

units.why: After a report, "The student is notified of the allegation" and "provided information regarding the process and their rights", and may "Respond to the information presented". This gives accused students a chance to respond, P64.
units.anchor: Respond to the information presented

units.why: The page states that "The conduct process is educational in nature and seeks to balance accountability, fairness, and student development." That treats misuse response as educative, P68.
units.anchor: The conduct process is educational in nature

units.why: "Faculty generally retain authority over academic decisions" such as "Grade reductions", "Assignment failure" and "Course failure". It names possible penalties and who decides, so P37 is nearest; no penalty is fixed for AI misuse, hence a partial fit.
units.anchor: Faculty generally retain authority over academic decisions within the course
units.fit_note: Lists possible academic outcomes and says faculty decide them; it does not set a specific penalty for AI misuse.

units.why: Outcomes should weigh "mitigating and aggravating circumstances such as prior conduct history or egregiousness". No existing type covers proportionality of sanctions, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: consider mitigating and aggravating circumstances such as prior conduct history
units.uncovered_note: When deciding outcomes for misconduct, weigh mitigating and aggravating circumstances such as prior history and how serious the violation is.

units.why: Faculty are encouraged to "Avoid making assumptions before reviewing all available information". It guards against unfounded accusations, which is closest to P69 (evidence standards); it is general, not AI-specific.
units.anchor: Avoid making assumptions before reviewing all available information
units.fit_note: Asks for review of all information before judging; no standard of proof is set.

units.why: "Maintain confidentiality throughout the process" is a conduct rule for staff handling cases. No type covers case confidentiality, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: Maintain confidentiality throughout the process
units.uncovered_note: Faculty keep misconduct cases confidential throughout the process.

units.why: Faculty should "Consult with the Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities when questions arise". It names the office that advises on and handles cases, a close match to P80 (who owns and enforces).
units.anchor: Consult with the Office of Student Rights and Responsibilities when questions arise
units.frag_start: Consult with the Office of Student
units.fit_note: Names the office to consult; the page does not say the office owns an AI policy.

units.why: The office "can provide" "Academic integrity presentations for students or departments". This is training offered to students, P70 (P63 is faculty-only).
units.anchor: Academic integrity presentations for students or departments
units.frag_start: The Office of Student Rights and
units.fit_note: Academic integrity training in general, not AI literacy specifically.

units.why: The office offers "Support with syllabus language and prevention strategies" and says "Departments and faculty groups are encouraged to request training". Support for faculty is P63.
units.anchor: Support with syllabus language and prevention strategies
units.fit_note: Faculty support on integrity and syllabus language, not on learning AI tools.

notes: Only one included document. Page text includes site navigation, which was skipped. The page is general academic-misconduct guidance with AI as one thread; several units are not AI-specific and carry fit_notes.
